**Why this matters:** Session 1 starts from the idea that open science is no longer optional. This reading gives
you the policy background and the common barriers, so the session can spend its time on FAIR, CARE and hands-on
practice. About 10 minutes.

## What is open science?

"Open science" is the umbrella value system for data best practices, which at their core help facilitate
collaborative science. You will also see it called *open research*. The Turing Way, a community-written handbook,
describes it this way ([The Turing Way Community, n.d.](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/open)):

> "Open research aims to transform research by making it more reproducible, transparent, reusable, collaborative,
> accountable, and accessible to society. It pushes for change in the way that research is carried out and
> disseminated by digital tools."

Many groups support researchers who want to work this way. [The Turing Way](https://book.the-turing-way.org) is a
community-written handbook on reproducible, ethical and collaborative data science.
[Openscapes](https://openscapes.org) is a movement that helps researchers connect and build confidence in open,
data-intensive science. NASA's Transform to Open Science (TOPS) initiative offers
[Open Science 101](https://science.data.nasa.gov/features-events/open-science-training), a free online course. For
Indigenous data governance, the [Global Indigenous Data Alliance (GIDA)](https://www.gida-global.org/careprinciples)
maintains the CARE principles, which we cover in the session.

## Open science in practice

Open science is no longer an optional "nice to have" aspect of research. Funders and journals increasingly require
shared data and metadata as part of the publication process.

Some requirements from [NSF's Public Access Policy](https://www.nsf.gov/policies/document/faq-public-access#qa-group-1)
include data management plans, machine-readable metadata, and for publications to be available free of charge. For
awards made on or after 22 January 2026, NSF also requires recipients to share all data supporting NSF-funded
publications at the time of publication, removes the 12-month embargo (a waiting period before a paper must be made
public), and moves the data management and sharing plan to a tool on Research.gov
([NSF 26-202](https://www.nsf.gov/policies/document/pappg24-1-supplement-2)).

[AGU's Position Statement on Data](https://www.agu.org/science-policy/position-statements/open-data) emphasizes
"Preserving Open Data as a World Heritage to Secure our Future", including topics like ensuring equitable access to
trusted and reusable data, implementing metadata standards across disciplines and domains, and taking collective
responsibility in maintaining data infrastructure.

## Barriers to open science

These barriers apply to open science in general, including the reproducibility practices covered in the session. For
more on these barriers and others not covered here, see
[The Turing Way](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/overview/overview-barriers/).

Putting your code and data online can be revealing and intimidating. Sharing possible errors in your work is a real
fear, but that is far outweighed by the feedback you may receive, and how you may help other scientists in their
research. It is also a motivator to hold your work to a higher standard which benefits all who are involved and all
who may learn from your work.

Working openly also takes additional time and effort, especially at the start of a project: setting up version
control, writing tests for your code, and agreeing with collaborators on what will be shared, when, and how. That
time pays off later. When a reviewer requests a change, version-controlled data and code make it much quicker to
integrate, and because others can see how the work was done, they can check it and build on it.

Some barriers are bigger than any one person. Journals tend to favor novel results, reproducible practices are often
not valued for promotion, and the skills involved take time to learn
([Whitaker, 2019](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2669547)). You can't fix these alone. That is a good reason to start
with the steps you can control, and to support change in your team and institution where you can.

## Putting open science into practice

It is easy to talk about open science, and more difficult to pull these practices into your own work. Here are some
tangible ways to start:

- **Opt for constructive peer code reviews during the development phase.** We are human and it is important to
  foster an environment where everyone is comfortable sharing in-progress work for constructive feedback. It is often
  the best way to ensure quality and build confidence in your work.
- **Share work early and often with peers and collaborators.** In every phase of the scientific process, it is
  important to get other people's perspectives. They may think of an issue you've run into from another angle and
  help you find a solution that you may never have thought of.
- **Publish data and code as their own citable products.** This makes your data, code, and findings accessible to
  the wider water science community. It may add an extra step to the process, but it will in turn lower the barrier
  of entry for someone that is building off of concepts related to your work. It also ensures that if someone does
  use your data or code, you will be properly credited.

## Key terms

- **Embargo:** a set period during which a dataset's or paper's files are withheld from the public, although its
  record (and often its DOI) can already be found.
- **Metadata:** data about data: what the values are, their units and definitions, where and when they were
  collected, how they were produced and who to contact.
- **Data management plan (DMP or DMSP):** a short document, written before a project starts, describing what data
  it will create or use and how they will be stored, documented, shared and preserved.
